about.summary_plain: Fits a model with each combination of the settings that you list. It scores each combination on a backtest and selects the best.

about.title: Summarise the parameters
about.summary_plain: Gives the estimate, the spread and the credible range of each parameter of a fitted Bayesian model, with checks that the sampler converged.
use_when: You want to branch on a parameter, for example when its range excludes zero
You must stop when the sampler did not converge (R-hat, effective sample size)
avoid_when: Models that give only point estimates (the node needs draws)
data_needs: A model version with posterior draws
assumptions: The draws come from two or more chains (else R-hat is not available)

references.title: Vehtari, Gelman, Simpson, Carpenter & Bürkner (2021), Rank-normalization, folding, and localization: an improved R-hat

about.expert_notes: Rank-normalised split R-hat (the larger of bulk and tail) and bulk ESS (Vehtari et al. 2021); the HDI is the narrowest interval with hdi_prob of the draws (0.94 gives the 3% and 97% bounds). Vector parameters are flattened to name[label] (labels of several dims joined by ', '), at most 200 values; max_rhat and min_ess check all the values (up to 20 000). Read the values with nodes.<id>.params['beta[north]'].hdi_low. n_divergent is null when the model stores no sample_stats. focus names one value (beta[north], or only north when one selected variable has that label), so a condition can read nodes.<id>.focus.excludes_zero when the label comes from a workflow parameter.

coverage_90.description: The share of observed values in the 90% range

about.title: Check the predictions against the data
about.summary_plain: Simulates new data from a fitted Bayesian model and compares it with the observed data. It shows if the model can make data that looks like the real data.
use_when: After each Bayesian fit, before you trust its ranges
You must stop a workflow when the model does not agree with the data
avoid_when: Models that give only point estimates or summaries (the node needs draws)
data_needs: A model version that predicts with draws
assumptions: The check uses the fit data, so it is optimistic (a model that overfits can pass)
outputs: The coverage of the 50% and 90% ranges, the PIT distance, a p-value and a verdict
about.example: 88% of the values are in the 90% range and p = 0.41 for the mean: the check passes.

references.title: Gelman, Meng & Stern (1996), Posterior predictive assessment of model fitness
Gabry et al. (2019), Visualization in Bayesian workflow

about.expert_notes: Posterior predictive draws come from the score path (predict, output kind predictive) on the fit data. coverage_p is the share of observations inside the central p interval of their predictive draws; pit_ks is the Kolmogorov-Smirnov distance of the PIT values P(y_rep < y) + 0.5 P(y_rep = y) from uniform, with the limit 1.36 / sqrt(n) unless pit_ks_max is set; the p-value is P(T(y_rep) >= T(y)) for T = statistic. ok needs both coverages within coverage_tolerance of nominal, the p-value in [p_min, 1 - p_min] and pit_ks under its limit.

about.summary_plain: Gives each candidate model a weight from how well it predicts each data point that it did not see. A mix of the models with these weights predicts best.

You want to average the predictions of the models, not select one of them
avoid_when: The models used different data (the scores are not comparable)
data_needs: Metrics of two or more model.fit nodes with evaluate: {metrics: [elpd_loo]}
assumptions: All candidates are fitted on the same data points in the same order
outputs: A weight for each candidate, the best candidate and a table
about.example: Weights: bym2 0.71, icar 0.29, iid 0.00.

references.title: Yao, Vehtari, Simpson & Gelman (2018), Using stacking to average Bayesian predictive distributions

about.expert_notes: Stacking maximises sum_i log sum_k w_k exp(elpd_loo_ik) over the simplex (Yao, Vehtari, Simpson & Gelman 2018), from the pointwise PSIS-LOO values that model.fit stores for data of at most 10 000 points. pseudo_bma (always reported) is pseudo-BMA+: softmax weights averaged over a Bayesian bootstrap of the pointwise elpd. Without pointwise values the weights are pseudo-BMA from elpd ± se (method pseudo_bma_se) or from elpd alone (pseudo_bma), and note_plain says so.

about.title: Time-series readiness to ARIMAX
about.summary_plain: Finds whether your series needs a difference and how many past values are important. Then it backtests a forecast with drivers against simple benchmarks and keeps the model only if it wins and passes governance.
use_when: You want an automatic, fully tested forecast of one series with drivers
You want a record and an explanation of each decision about the model
avoid_when: You have many related series that affect each other (use VAR or VECM)
You have less than about two seasons of history
data_needs: One numeric series over time, at least two seasons long
Optional drivers that you know for the future (for example, prices and holidays)
assumptions: Past patterns continue into the forecast horizon
The drivers have a linear effect on the series
outputs: Test verdicts and the decision about the difference
The selected AR and MA orders
Backtest errors for each horizon, compared with the benchmarks
A validated ARIMAX model
A plain-language report
about.example: Weekly orders: the tests say 'difference once' and AIC selects (2,1,1). The backtest is 25% better than seasonal naive, and governance passes.

references.title: Hyndman & Athanasopoulos, Forecasting: Principles and Practice

alpha.description: The significance level of the tests

season.description: The length of a season in periods (52 for weekly data)

horizons.description: The forecast horizons that the backtest scores

gap.description: The periods between the training data and the test data (for late data)

drivers.description: The driver columns that you know for the future

with.explain_then: The series has a strong seasonal pattern. The workflow compared each value with the same period one season earlier (a seasonal difference).
with.explain_else: The series has no strong seasonal pattern, so the workflow did not apply a seasonal difference.

with.condition: (not nodes.adf.reject or nodes.kpss.reject) and not (nodes.pp.reject and nodes.za.reject) and nodes.overdiff.acf[1] > -0.5
with.explain_then: The tests found that the series wanders and does not return to a steady level. The workflow applied a difference, so the model uses the change from one period to the next.
with.explain_else: The tests found that the series returns to a steady level, or that a difference would go too far. The workflow used the series as it is.

about.title: Series that move together (VAR or VECM)

avoid_when: A single series
Less than about 50 periods
data_needs: Two to five numeric series over time at the same frequency. Each series has one value for each period (a long table, or a wide sheet that you ingest with the wide mapping)
assumptions: The relationships stay the same over the period
Effects come from past values
outputs: The cointegration rank
A VECM or VAR model
Granger test results
A report
about.example: Your price and the prices of two competitors share one long-run tie. A VECM with rank 1 shows that the gaps close in less than one month.

target.description: The main result (one of the series)

driver.description: A series that can possibly help to predict the target

data.description: The series along one dimension (one value for each series and period)

with.explain_then: The test found that the series stay tied together in the long run. The workflow fitted a model that keeps that tie (VECM).
with.explain_else: The test found no long-run tie between the series, so the workflow fitted a VAR and not a VECM.

The model risk team or the auditors need evidence
avoid_when: You only want a quick look at the data (use the guided template)

avoid_when: You already have a model that you trust

assumptions: The backtest periods are similar to the future

The winner, fitted again
A comparison report

about.title: Disease map: which spatial model?
about.summary_plain: Fits three models of disease counts on a map, from independent areas to areas that share their risk with their neighbours. Then it compares how well each model predicts, keeps the best one and tells you if the effect of your covariate stays clear.
use_when: You have counts and expected counts for each area of a map, and one covariate
You must know if the neighbours of an area change the answer
You need a map of the risk with evidence that the fit is good
avoid_when: You have the location of each case, not counts for each area
The areas have no neighbours (all of them are islands)
You need a fast answer (the workflow fits the model three times. When the effect is clear, it fits the best model two more times)
data_needs: A count of cases and an expected count for each area
One covariate for each area, for example a percentage
An adjacency matrix of the areas and the outline of each area (python -m mapi_plugin_science.export e18 makes this dataset from the Scottish lip cancer data)
assumptions: All three models use the same areas in the same order
The covariate has the same effect in every area
Leave-one-area-out scores (PSIS-LOO) are reliable for these data. The comparison table shows a warning when they are not
outputs: A table that compares the three models (elpd_loo) and their stacking weights
The best model, with the range of the covariate effect and a decision: clear or not clear
Convergence evidence for the best model
When the effect is clear, the range of the effect with wider and narrower priors
A map of the relative risk and a report with the plot
about.example: On the 56 districts of Scotland, the effect of outdoor work on the log risk falls from 0.67 (independent areas) to 0.40 (BYM2) per 10 points when the areas share their risk. The workflow shows which model predicts best and if the effect stays clear.

references.title: Riebler, Sørbye, Simpson & Rue (2016), An intuitive Bayesian spatial model for disease mapping that accounts for scaling
Yao, Vehtari, Simpson & Gelman (2018), Using stacking to average Bayesian predictive distributions

about.expert_notes: Poisson(E_i exp(b0 + b1 x_i + u_i)) with u iid, ICAR or BYM2 (scaled ICAR plus iid with mixing share rho). Each rung stores the pointwise PSIS-LOO values, so compare.stacking solves the stacking weights over the same areas. The branch reads the HDI of b1 on the rung that select.best keeps. When it excludes zero, that rung is fitted again with the prior sds of b0 and b1 and the HalfNormal scale of sigma multiplied and divided by prior_scale.

bind.description: The names in your dataset of the area dims and of the covariate (the default fits the e18 export)

islands.description: What to do with areas that have no neighbours. link_nearest links each one to the area with the closest border

hdi_prob.description: The probability inside the range of each parameter

prior_scale.description: When the effect is clear, the workflow fits the best model again with the prior widths multiplied and divided by this value

draws.description: The posterior draws to keep in each chain

tune.description: The warm-up steps of each chain (the sampler discards them)

chains.description: The number of chains (two or more, for R-hat)

target_accept.description: The target acceptance rate of the sampler. A higher value gives smaller steps and fewer divergences

engine.description: The sampler (nutpie is faster on large data)

seed.description: The random seed of each fit

data.description: Counts, expected counts, a covariate, the adjacency matrix and the outlines of the areas

with.explain_then: The range of the covariate effect in the best model does not include zero. The covariate has a clear effect on the risk. The workflow fits the best model again with wider and narrower priors.
with.explain_else: The range of the covariate effect in the best model includes zero. When the areas share their risk, the data does not show a clear effect of the covariate.

with.title: Relative risk of each area (best model)

about.title: Network ties: which model?
about.summary_plain: Fits three models of the ties in a network, from shared traits only to a hidden map of the group. Then it compares how well each model predicts, keeps the best one and simulates new networks to compare them with your network.
use_when: You have a table of yes or no ties between the pairs of a group, for example who works with whom
You want to know if shared traits explain the ties, or if the activity of each node and a hidden map are necessary
You need simulated networks to do a check of the model fit
avoid_when: The ties have a direction or are counts
The network has many thousands of nodes (each model looks at every pair)
You need a fast answer (the workflow fits the model three times)
data_needs: A square table with 1 for a tie, 0 for no tie and an empty cell when you do not know
Values for each pair, for example 1 when the two nodes are in the same office
Optional: a group code for each node, for colors in the plots (python -m mapi_plugin_science.export e21 makes this dataset from the law firm data)
assumptions: All three models use the same pairs in the same order
Each pair has a tie or not, and the two directions are the same
Leave-one-pair-out scores (PSIS-LOO) are reliable for these data. The comparison table shows a warning when they are not
outputs: A table that compares the three models (elpd_loo) and their stacking weights
The best model, with the range of each pair effect
A plot of the network with the tie probabilities of the best model
Statistics of simulated networks (density, transitivity and more) with a plot
A report with the plots
about.example: On the coworker network of 71 lawyers, the hidden map predicts best (elpd_loo -761.6, against -763.4 with activity and -894.2 with covariates only). The simulated networks show if the model makes as many triangles as the real network.

references.title: Hoff, Raftery & Handcock (2002), Latent space approaches to social network analysis

about.expert_notes: Bernoulli-logit dyad models: covariates (alpha + x beta), sociality (+ s_i + s_j) and latent_space (- ||z_i - z_j||, Procrustes-aligned). The log-likelihood is over the observed pairs i < j, so the pointwise PSIS-LOO values of the rungs line up for stacking. model.score in simulate mode draws whole graphs from the best rung and returns graph_stat(statistic) for each draw.

about.title: Trait regression across species, with and without the tree
about.summary_plain: Fits the same regression of a species trait four times: once with species as independent points and three times with a family tree that relates them. Then it keeps the version that predicts best and tells you if the effect that you ask about is clearly different from zero.
use_when: You compare a trait across species (or other groups with a known tree) and close relatives are similar
You want to know if an effect stays clear when you include the tree in the model
avoid_when: You have no tree of the species
Fewer than about 20 species (the four versions then predict about equally well)
data_needs: One row for each species: the trait to explain and one or more predictors, all positive (the model takes logs)
The tree in the same dataset: parent(node), branch_length(node), is_tip(node) and tip_label(node), with tip labels equal to the species labels
assumptions: The predictors have a linear effect on the log of the trait
The residuals of related species are correlated as the selected version says (Brownian motion, Pagel's lambda or Ornstein-Uhlenbeck)
outputs: The leave-one-out score (elpd_loo) of the four versions and their stacking weights
The selected model and its slopes, with R-hat and ESS
The decision: is the range of the effect clear of zero?
A plot of the tree with the trait of each species
A report
about.example: Brain size of 301 primates: Pagel's lambda wins (elpd 130, against 15 without the tree). The slope of group size is 0.03, with the 94% range -0.01 to 0.07. Thus the effect is not clear of zero when the model includes the tree.

references.title: Felsenstein (1985), Phylogenies and the comparative method
Pagel (1999), Inferring the historical patterns of biological evolution

about.expert_notes: Four sci.phylo_regression fits that differ only in the residual kind (iid, brownian, lambda, ou) are ranked by PSIS-LOO on the conditional leave-one-out density of each species. select.best keeps the highest elpd_loo, and compare.stacking gives the stacking weights. model.summary reads the slope that focus names from the winner. The branch tests if its HDI excludes zero.

about.title: Calibrate a heated plate, then test a heater layout
about.summary_plain: Learns how a plate conducts and loses heat from some test runs with thermocouples. Then it predicts the temperature of each point of the plate for a new heater layout, but only if the calibration predicts a test run that it did not see well enough.
use_when: You measured a plate (or a similar flat part) with one heater layout for each run and some thermocouples
You want to try a new heater layout on the computer before you build it
avoid_when: The heat does not reach a steady state in your runs
Fewer than three calibration runs (one run is held out for the test)
data_needs: The calibration runs: heater_power(run, y, x) in W and temperature(run, y, x) in degC on a regular grid, with no value where there is no thermocouple
Optional: a second dataset with heater_power(run, y, x) of the new layouts on the same grid (without one, the workflow predicts the calibration runs)
assumptions: The plate is thin and reaches a steady state (the 2-D steady heat equation)
The material and the losses are the same in each run
The temperature rise is proportional to the heater power
outputs: The conductivity k, the face and edge losses, the heater efficiency and the spread length, with R-hat and ESS
The error on the calibration run that the fit did not see
The decision: is the calibration good enough?

about.title: Bayesian workflow audit
about.summary_plain: Fits a Bayesian model and does each check of a careful workflow: the starting assumptions, the sampler, the predictions, the effect of the priors and the recovery of known values. Then it writes one report with the plots.

A reviewer asks for the standard checks of a Bayesian workflow
You changed a model and want to do all the checks again

about.title: Better than shuffled data
about.summary_plain: Fits the model again on copies of the data where the drivers have a random time order. A real model must be clearly better on the true data than on the shuffled copies.

avoid_when: Models without a test period (there is nothing to compare)

assumptions: A random order of the drivers removes each real link between the drivers and the result

about.expert_notes: Permutation (randomisation) test on a scale-free statistic: holdout skill 1 - L(model) / L(null forecast) on each dataset (the null forecast is the last training value of an integrated series, else its mean). about.title: Marketing mix model
about.summary_plain: Measures how much each marketing channel adds to your sales, in total or for each market. It also shows what occurs if you move budget between channels.
use_when: You have two or more years of weekly sales and spend for each channel
You want to know the return of each channel and plan budgets
You have results for each market or product and you want one model for all of them
avoid_when: Spend changes very little over time (the model cannot measure the effect)
You have less than a year of history
You need answers in seconds (use the fast frequentist version)
data_needs: Weekly (or daily) sales, spend for each channel, and optional controls such as price
assumptions: Advertising has an effect that continues for some time, and diminishing returns
The controls include the factors that change both spend and sales
outputs: Contribution and return for each channel, with ranges
Response curves
Budget plans and what-if answers
about.example: TV returns 2.1 euros for each euro of spend (range 1.4 to 2.9) and search returns 3.4.

references.title: Jin et al. (2017), Bayesian methods for media mix modeling with carryover and shape effects

about.expert_notes: mmm-framework BayesianMMM: geometric/Weibull adstock, Hill or logistic saturation, trend options, Fourier seasonality, and hierarchical pooling over geos and products (MFF panels). Priors come from business beliefs. Lift tests are a calibration likelihood. NUTS through PyMC, nutpie or numpyro.

about.title: Fast marketing mix model
about.summary_plain: Gives a quick first estimate of the contribution of each channel in seconds. Its ranges (from resampled data) are simpler than the uncertainty of a full Bayesian model.
use_when: You need a fast first look before a full model
You want to compare many set-ups quickly
avoid_when: Decisions depend on the full uncertainty of the answer (use the Bayesian model)
You want to add business beliefs or lift tests
data_needs: Weekly sales and spend for each channel
assumptions: The model searches a grid for the carry-over and saturation settings
Channel effects are not negative
outputs: Contribution and return for each channel, with bootstrap ranges
about.example: A first result in 5 seconds: TV 28% of sales, search 12%.
about.expert_notes: mmm-framework frequentist ridge / constrained least squares with a grid search over transform parameters. Block-bootstrap replicates (a minimum of 20) are the draws of each output, so its ranges are confidence intervals, not posteriors.

about.title: Predict a number with ranges you can add up
about.summary_plain: Fits the same method many times on resampled data. This gives ranges that stay correct when you add predictions into totals.
use_when: You need a range for totals (all stores, a full region)
The data has groups (stores) that the resample must keep together
avoid_when: You need results in seconds on a very large table (it fits many models)
data_needs: A table of the number to predict and the columns that explain it
assumptions: The rows that you predict are similar to the rows that the model learned from
A resample of full groups shows how uncertain the model is
outputs: Many joint simulated predictions for each row
Ranges for all totals
about.example: A range for the total sales of next month across 300 stores.
about.expert_notes: A bootstrap ensemble (with an optional resample of full groups with 'by'). Each replicate is a joint draw, so aggregation is valid (draws representation).

about.title: Predict yes or no
about.summary_plain: Estimates the probability that something occurs for each row of a table. For example, a customer buys again or an order arrives late.
use_when: The result is yes or no for each row
You want a probability to put rows in order or to select rows
avoid_when: The result is a number or has more than two outcomes
data_needs: A table with a yes/no column and the columns that explain it
assumptions: The rows that you score are similar to the rows that the model learned from
outputs: The probability of 'yes' for each row
about.example: The probability that each customer orders again next month, to decide who gets a voucher.
about.expert_notes: An allow-listed scikit-learn or xgboost binary classifier on stacked rows. Point representation of the positive-class probability.

about.title: Predict a number with a guaranteed range
about.summary_plain: Predicts a number for each row with a range. The range contains the true value about as frequently as you ask, such as nine times in ten.
use_when: You need ranges with a coverage that you can trust for each row
You do not want to make assumptions about the shape of the errors
avoid_when: You need ranges for totals (use the bootstrap version)
You have very little data (the model keeps a part of it to set the size of the ranges)
data_needs: A table of the number to predict and the columns that explain it
assumptions: New rows behave like the rows that the model kept to set the size of the ranges
outputs: One prediction and a range for each row
about.example: Ranges that contain the demand of next week for 90% of store-product pairs.
about.expert_notes: Split-conformal prediction intervals at level 1 - alpha with a calibration fraction. Marginal coverage for each cell. Interval representation (you cannot aggregate it).

about.title: Predict a number with a low and high estimate
about.summary_plain: Predicts a low, middle and high value for each row of a table. These values show how certain the prediction is.
use_when: You need a best case and a worst case for each store, product or customer
Stock or staff decisions depend on the high end or the low end
avoid_when: You need to add predictions into totals with a range (you cannot add the ranges of rows)
data_needs: A table of the number to predict and the columns that explain it
assumptions: The rows that you predict are similar to the rows that the model learned from
outputs: A low, middle and high prediction for each row
about.example: Plan stock at the 90% level: the high estimate of the demand of next week for each store.
about.expert_notes: xgboost multi-quantile regression or one scikit-learn quantile model for each level. Quantile representation (you cannot aggregate the quantiles of cells across cells).

about.title: Predict a number from a table
about.summary_plain: Predicts a number for each row of a table, such as a store and week, from the other columns. It uses a well-known machine-learning method that you select.
use_when: You have many rows with drivers (price, promotion, weather) and you want one best estimate for each row
You want to see how much each driver adds to a prediction
avoid_when: You need a range of probable values (use the quantile, bootstrap or conformal versions)
You have one short series over time
data_needs: A table of the number to predict and the columns that explain it
assumptions: The rows that you predict are similar to the rows that the model learned from
You know the future values of the drivers when you forecast
outputs: One prediction for each row
The contribution of each driver (linear and tree models)
about.example: Predict the units of next week for each store and product from planned prices, with gradient boosting.
about.expert_notes: An allow-listed scikit-learn or xgboost regressor on rows stacked from the labelled dims (coordinates become features). Point representation. Exact linear or counterfactual-zeroing contributions. The server stores models as skops or xgboost JSON.

about.title: Group effects with sharing
about.summary_plain: Estimates a separate baseline for each group, such as a county or a store. Small groups get help from the data of the other groups.
use_when: Groups have very different quantities of data
You want to predict for groups that the model did not see
avoid_when: You have one series over time
data_needs: One row for each observation with a group label and predictors
assumptions: Groups are sufficiently similar to share information
Effects are additive on the scale of the model
outputs: Effects for each group with ranges
Predictions for new groups
about.example: Radon levels for each house. If a county has few houses, its baseline moves towards the state average.
about.expert_notes: Bayesian hierarchical GLM (PyMC, NUTS). Partially pooled group intercepts and optional slopes. Group-level covariates in the mean. The model draws new levels from the fitted hyperprior.

about.title: Demand by store and week
about.summary_plain: Predicts a number for each store, product and week from prices, promotions and the calendar. It gives a low and a high estimate.
use_when: You have many stores or products and you want a forecast for each
Prices, promotions or stock explain demand
avoid_when: You need to add predictions into totals with a range (you cannot add ranges)
You have one short series
data_needs: A table of the number to predict and its drivers, for each store and week
assumptions: You know the future values of the drivers when you forecast
Stores that the model did not see behave like the average store
outputs: A median forecast with low and high values for each cell
Feature importance
about.example: Predict the units of next week for 300 stores from planned prices and promotions.
about.expert_notes: Gradient-boosted quantile regression (xgboost or sklearn) on stacked rows. Coordinates become categorical features. Direct multi-horizon forecasting. Quantile representation (no cross-cell aggregation).

about.title: Effects that build up over time
about.summary_plain: Explains a series from its past and from the current and past values of drivers. You can see how an effect increases over several periods.
use_when: The effect of a driver spreads over several periods
avoid_when: Effects are only immediate (a simple regression is sufficient)
data_needs: One result and one or more drivers over time
assumptions: The drivers change the result, but the result does not change the drivers
The series vary around stable levels or share a long-run relationship
outputs: Effects for each lag
Long-run multipliers
Forecasts for given future drivers
about.example: A promotion increases sales by 8% in its week and by 3% in the next week.
about.expert_notes: statsmodels ARDL with lag orders that an information criterion selects (ardl_select_order).

about.title: Forecast from past values
about.summary_plain: Forecasts a series from its recent past and trend, without outside drivers.
use_when: You have only the series
You want a reliable, well-known forecast method
avoid_when: Outside drivers explain most of the movement (use the version with drivers)
data_needs: One number over time at a regular frequency
assumptions: After differencing, the series varies around a stable level
outputs: A forecast with a range
Residual checks
about.example: Forecast monthly sales 6 months ahead from the sales of recent years.
about.expert_notes: statsmodels ARIMA(p,d,q)(P,D,Q)s (state space) without exog.

about.title: Common movements across many series
about.summary_plain: Finds a few hidden forces that move many series together, such as the general economy behind the sales in many categories.
use_when: You have many related series and you want their shared drivers
avoid_when: You have one or two series
data_needs: Many numbers over time at the same frequency
assumptions: Some common factors explain most of the joint movement
outputs: The common factors over time
How much each series follows them
Forecasts
about.example: Twenty series of category sales follow one 'consumer mood' factor.
about.expert_notes: statsmodels DynamicFactor (state space; the factors follow a VAR).

about.title: Long-run and short-run effects
about.summary_plain: Separates the short-term effect of a driver from its long-term effect on one series. It also tests if a long-run relationship exists.
use_when: One result and some drivers have the same trend
You want both the immediate effect and the lasting effect of a driver
avoid_when: The result and the drivers do not have a trend (a regression with lags is sufficient)
data_needs: One result and one or more drivers over time
assumptions: The drivers change the result, but the result does not change the drivers
outputs: Short-run and long-run effects
Speed of adjustment
A bounds test result
about.example: A 1% price increase decreases sales by 0.4% immediately and by 1.1% in the long run.

references.title: Pesaran, Shin & Smith (2001), Bounds testing approaches

about.expert_notes: Single-equation error-correction model in UECM form (statsmodels UECM). Pesaran-Shin-Smith bounds test for a levels relationship.

about.title: Exponential smoothing forecast
about.summary_plain: Forecasts a series and gives recent values more weight than older values. It has an optional trend and seasonality, and it is quick and robust.
use_when: You need a fast, reliable baseline forecast
The level, trend and seasonality change slowly
avoid_when: Outside drivers explain most of the movement
data_needs: One number over time at a regular frequency
assumptions: Recent history is the best guide to the near future
outputs: A forecast with a range
Level, trend and seasonal parts
about.example: Forecast monthly demand 12 months ahead with a damped trend.

references.title: Hyndman et al., Forecasting with Exponential Smoothing

about.expert_notes: statsmodels ETSModel (error, trend, seasonal; additive or multiplicative; damped trend), with prediction intervals from simulation.

about.title: Hidden states over time
about.summary_plain: Finds a small number of hidden states, such as calm periods and busy periods, that a series changes between. It tells you the probable state of each period.
use_when: Your series seems to change between distinct modes
avoid_when: Behaviour changes smoothly, not in jumps
You have very short sequences
data_needs: One or more sequences of measurements over time
assumptions: Each state has its own typical level and spread
The probability of a change of state depends only on the current state
outputs: The probable state of each period
How frequently the states change
Forecasts
about.example: The track of an animal divides into rest phases and travel phases.
about.expert_notes: K-state Gaussian HMM. The forward algorithm in PyMC marginalises the states. The terminal state is stored for forecast and filter. Ordering fixes label switching.

about.title: Smooth trend forecast
about.summary_plain: Forecasts one regular series with a smooth, flexible trend and a repeating seasonal pattern. It gives a range of probable values.
use_when: You forecast one weekly or daily series with a trend that bends over time
You want an honest range around the forecast
avoid_when: You have many related series (forecast them together or for each store)
You need a forecast further ahead than the model permits without a new fit
data_needs: One number over time at a regular frequency
assumptions: The trend changes gradually
The seasonal pattern repeats
outputs: A forecast with a range
Trend and seasonal parts
about.example: Forecast weekly website visits 26 weeks ahead with a 90% range.

references.title: Riutort-Mayol et al. (2022), Practical Hilbert space approximate Bayesian Gaussian processes

about.expert_notes: Hilbert-space Gaussian process (HSGP) trend with optional linear drift and Fourier seasonality (PyMC, NUTS). Forecasts are limited to max_extension periods.

about.title: Changes between regimes
about.summary_plain: Finds if a series changes between regimes, such as periods of high growth and low growth. It estimates the behaviour in each regime.
use_when: Behaviour seems to jump between distinct modes
You want the probability of each mode now
avoid_when: Changes are gradual
You have little history
data_needs: One number over time, and optional drivers
assumptions: There is a small number of regimes. A change of regime depends only on the current regime
outputs: The probability of each regime for each period
Behaviour in each regime
about.example: Demand changes between a normal regime and a regime that promotions cause.

references.title: Hamilton (1989), A new approach to the economic analysis of nonstationary time series

about.expert_notes: statsmodels MarkovRegression / MarkovAutoregression (Hamilton filter, EM then BFGS).

about.title: Forecast with past values and drivers
about.summary_plain: Forecasts a series from its recent past, its seasonal pattern and outside drivers that you know in advance, such as planned prices or holidays.
use_when: You forecast one regular series some periods ahead
Known future drivers (prices, promotions, holidays) are important
avoid_when: You have less than about 50 periods
Two or more series change each other (use VAR)
data_needs: One number over time at a regular frequency, and optional driver columns that you know for the future
assumptions: After differencing, the series varies around a stable level
Relationships stay the same over time
outputs: A forecast with a range
Effects of the drivers
Residual checks
about.example: Forecast weekly orders 12 weeks ahead from the orders of recent weeks and planned discounts.

references.title: Hyndman & Athanasopoulos, Forecasting: Principles and Practice (ch. 9-10)

about.expert_notes: statsmodels SARIMAX (state space): ARIMA(p,d,q)(P,D,Q)s with exogenous regressors. Exact likelihood through the Kalman filter. Prediction intervals as quantiles. Forecasts need future exog.

about.title: Simple strong baseline
about.summary_plain: Forecasts a series with a combination of a straight-line trend and smoothed recent values. This simple method is hard to beat.
use_when: You want a strong, simple baseline to compare with other models
avoid_when: Outside drivers are very important
You need detailed explanations
data_needs: One number over time (the model removes the seasonality and puts it back automatically)
assumptions: The recent trend continues
outputs: A forecast with a range
about.example: A theta forecast of monthly sales that other models must beat before you use them.
about.expert_notes: statsmodels ThetaModel (Assimakopoulos-Nikolopoulos; equivalent to SES with drift) with optional seasonal decomposition.

about.title: Trend, season and noise
about.summary_plain: Divides a series into a level and a trend that change slowly, a seasonal pattern and noise. It forecasts the series from these parts.
use_when: You want to see the underlying trend without the noise
The trend and the season change slowly over time
avoid_when: You only need a quick baseline (exponential smoothing is simpler)
data_needs: One number over time, and optional drivers
assumptions: Each part changes smoothly and independently
outputs: Smoothed level, trend and season
Forecasts with ranges
about.example: Weekly sales divide into an increasing trend, a Christmas peak and noise from week to week.

references.title: Harvey, Forecasting, Structural Time Series Models and the Kalman Filter

about.expert_notes: statsmodels UnobservedComponents (local level/trend, stochastic seasonal, cycle, exog), estimated by maximum likelihood with the Kalman smoother.

about.title: Series that drive each other
about.summary_plain: Models two or more series that change each other over time, such as the prices and sales of two brands. It forecasts them together.
use_when: Two or more series move together and change each other
You want to see how a shock to one series goes to the other series
avoid_when: You have one series
The series have the same trend permanently (use the error-correction model)
data_needs: Two or more numbers over time at the same frequency
assumptions: Each series varies around a stable level, after differencing if necessary
Effects work through past values
outputs: Joint forecasts with ranges
How a shock goes through the series (impulse responses)
Which series help to predict which series (Granger tests)
about.example: A price decrease by brand A decreases the sales of brand B for three weeks.

references.title: Lutkepohl, New Introduction to Multiple Time Series Analysis

about.expert_notes: statsmodels VAR(p): OLS for each equation. Lag order by AIC/BIC/HQIC. Impulse responses and forecast-error variance decomposition. Granger causality tests.

about.title: Series that drive each other, with drivers
about.summary_plain: Models two or more series that change each other and also respond to outside drivers that you know in advance. It forecasts them together.
use_when: Two or more series change each other, and outside drivers are also important
avoid_when: You have one series
You have many series and little history
data_needs: Two or more numbers over time, and driver columns that you know for the future
assumptions: Series vary around stable levels
Driver effects are steady
outputs: Joint forecasts with ranges
Driver effects
Impulse responses
about.example: Forecast the sales of two brands from the history of each brand and planned promotions.
about.expert_notes: statsmodels VARMAX(p,q) with exogenous regressors (VARX when q = 0), estimated by maximum likelihood in state-space form.

about.title: Series tied together in the long run
about.summary_plain: Models series that wander but stay tied together in the long run, such as the prices of close substitutes. It shows how fast they go back after a gap opens.
use_when: The series have a trend but keep a stable long-run relationship
avoid_when: The series do not have a trend
A long-run tie is not probable
data_needs: Two or more numbers with a trend over time
assumptions: A stable long-run relationship exists (the Johansen test does a check of this)
outputs: Long-run relationships
Speed of adjustment
Joint forecasts with ranges
about.example: When the price of a competitor goes 5% above your price, half of the gap closes in 4 weeks.

references.title: Johansen (1991), Estimation and hypothesis testing of cointegration vectors

about.expert_notes: statsmodels VECM with cointegration rank from the Johansen trace/max-eigenvalue tests. You can select the deterministic terms.

about.title: Decision
about.summary_plain: Uses earlier results to select the path of the workflow.
use_when: A step must run only when a condition is true
avoid_when: All steps always run
data_needs: The results of earlier nodes
assumptions: Conditions read only earlier results
outputs: The path that the workflow took
about.example: Apply a difference only when the series wanders.

about.title: Comparison
about.summary_plain: Puts the scores of several candidates side by side, or tests whether one candidate is really better.
use_when: Several candidate models
avoid_when: One candidate
data_needs: Metrics of the candidates
assumptions: The same folds for each candidate
outputs: A comparison table or a test
about.example: ARIMAX vs ETS vs naive.

about.title: Evaluation
about.summary_plain: Measures how good a model or a simple benchmark is on test data.
use_when: After you fit or backtest a model
avoid_when: No data was kept for the test
data_needs: Model versions or backtests
assumptions: The test data is similar to real use
outputs: Metrics
about.example: Score the seasonal-naive benchmark.

about.title: Governance
about.summary_plain: Runs the checks that a model must pass before you can validate it. It stores the evidence.
use_when: Before you validate or promote a model
avoid_when: Experiments that you will not keep
data_needs: A model version and its data
assumptions: A policy covers the model family
outputs: Evidence and a pass or fail
about.example: Run the tenant policy.

about.title: Model
about.summary_plain: Fits, backtests or forecasts with any model from the catalog.
use_when: The workflow must make a model or a forecast
avoid_when: Only checks of the data
data_needs: A dataset and model settings
assumptions: The assumptions of the model
outputs: Model versions, metrics and forecasts
about.example: Fit an ARIMAX model.

about.title: Plot
about.summary_plain: Draws a plot from the plot catalog in the run, for the run view and the report.
use_when: You want a chart in the run or in the report
avoid_when: Nobody reads the chart
data_needs: A model version or a dataset
assumptions: The recipe can read the data
outputs: A plot
about.example: Draw the forecast fan chart.

about.title: Report
about.summary_plain: Changes the results of the workflow into a report that is easy to read, or into an evidence pack.
use_when: You want to share the results
avoid_when: Nobody reads the result
data_needs: Earlier results
assumptions: Earlier nodes finished
outputs: A report
about.example: A one-page summary.

about.title: Search
about.summary_plain: Tries many settings and selects the best setting by a score.
use_when: You want to select orders or settings from the data
avoid_when: The settings are fixed before the run
data_needs: A dataset (and a split plan for backtest searches)
assumptions: The best setting is in the search range
outputs: The best settings and a table of scores
about.example: Find ARMA orders by AIC.

about.title: Selection
about.summary_plain: Selects the winner, or all candidates that pass a limit.
use_when: The end of a bake-off
avoid_when: One candidate
data_needs: A comparison table
assumptions: The metric agrees with the decision
outputs: The selected model(s)
about.example: The lowest RMSE wins.

about.title: Train/test plan
about.summary_plain: Decides which periods or groups the model learns from, and which periods or groups test the model. It can do this many times.
use_when: Each model that you want to test honestly
avoid_when: You do not test the model
data_needs: A dataset
assumptions: The test periods are similar to the real use of the model
outputs: A split plan
about.example: Six expanding-window folds.

about.title: Sub-workflow
about.summary_plain: Runs another saved workflow as one step.
use_when: You want to use a common sequence again
avoid_when: Steps that you use one time only
data_needs: A saved workflow revision
assumptions: The inputs and outputs agree
outputs: The outputs of the other workflow
about.example: Reuse the readiness checks.

about.title: Statistical test
about.summary_plain: Tests a property of the data or of the errors of a model. It gives a yes/no verdict with its evidence.
use_when: You must make a decision from the data (for example, about a difference or lags)
avoid_when: You only want a chart (use the Data Explorer)
data_needs: A dataset or a model version
assumptions: The assumptions of each test (see its card)
outputs: The statistic, the p-value, the decision and a plain verdict
about.example: ADF shows that the series wanders.

about.title: Data processing
about.summary_plain: Changes the data before later steps use it. For example, it calculates differences or logs.
use_when: You must prepare the data before a test or a model
avoid_when: The data is ready as it is
data_needs: A dataset
assumptions: The workflow reverses the transforms on forecasts where necessary
outputs: A new dataset
about.example: Apply one difference to sales.

about.title: Bayesian workflow audit
about.summary_plain: Fits a Bayesian model and does each check of a careful workflow: the starting assumptions, the sampler, the predictions, the effect of the priors and the recovery of known values. Then it writes one report with the plots.
use_when: You want to trust a Bayesian model before you use its ranges
A reviewer asks for the standard checks of a Bayesian workflow
You changed a model and want to do all the checks again
avoid_when: The model gives only point estimates (the checks need draws)
You need a result in seconds (the recovery check fits the model many times)
data_needs: A dataset that the model can fit
The model reference, its settings and, if the names are different, the binding of the dataset to the model
assumptions: The model gives posterior draws and can predict the fit data
The fit has two or more chains, so that the workflow can measure R-hat
outputs: A fitted model version
A table of the parameters with R-hat and the effective sample size
The coverage of the 50% and 90% ranges, the PIT distance and a p-value
The prior sensitivity and recovery evidence
A report with the prior predictive, pair, predictive and estimate plots
about.example: Radon in 85 counties: R-hat 1.00, 89% of the homes in the 90% ranges, and priors two times wider move the floor effect by 3%. The audit passes.

references.title: Gabry et al. (2019), Visualization in Bayesian workflow

about.expert_notes: The fit keeps prior_predictive.draws prior predictive draws for core.prior_predictive (set prior_predictive to {} for a model that cannot sample its priors, for example an ICAR prior). The branch 'converged' needs the largest R-hat (rank-normalised split R-hat over all the posterior values, up to 20 000) under rhat_max and the smallest bulk ESS at or over min_ess. Only then do evaluate.ppc, sensitivity.prior (refits with the prior widths times each of prior_scales) and recovery.simulated (n_sims refits on simulated targets, at the refit budget of the governance run) run. The branch 'trusted' needs ppc.ok and no fail or error from the two governance checks. A check that does not apply (skipped) does not block. The plots use on_failure: continue, so a recipe that cannot read a model gives a line in the report and does not stop the audit.

about.title: Forecast bake-off
about.summary_plain: Backtests some forecast models on the same periods and compares them with simple benchmarks. Then it fits the winner again.
use_when: You do not know which forecast method is best for your series
avoid_when: You already have a model that you trust
data_needs: One numeric series over time, at least two seasons long
assumptions: The backtest periods are similar to the future
outputs: Backtest errors for each model and horizon
The winner, fitted again
A comparison report
about.example: ETS wins with 7% error at 4 weeks. ARIMA has 8%, Theta 9% and seasonal naive 12%.

about.title: Marketing mix with governance
about.summary_plain: Does a check of your drivers and fits the marketing mix model. Then it runs the governance checks of your organisation and makes a report and an evidence pack for approval.
use_when: You will use a marketing mix model to make budget decisions
The model risk team or the auditors need evidence
avoid_when: You only want a quick look at the data (use the guided template)
data_needs: Weekly sales and the spend for each channel (for each market, if you have this data)
assumptions: Your organisation has a governance policy for marketing mix models
outputs: A fitted marketing mix model
Governance evidence
A report and an evidence pack
about.example: The model passes the shuffled-result and fake-channel checks. Then it waits for the approval of a reviewer.

about.title: Calibrate a heated plate, then test a heater layout
about.summary_plain: Learns how a plate conducts and loses heat from some test runs with thermocouples. Then it predicts the temperature of each point of the plate for a new heater layout, but only if the calibration predicts a test run that it did not see well enough.
use_when: You measured a plate (or a similar flat part) with one heater layout for each run and some thermocouples
You want to try a new heater layout on the computer before you build it
avoid_when: The heat does not reach a steady state in your runs
Fewer than three calibration runs (one run is held out for the test)
data_needs: The calibration runs: heater_power(run, y, x) in W and temperature(run, y, x) in degC on a regular grid, with no value where there is no thermocouple
Optional: a second dataset with heater_power(run, y, x) of the new layouts on the same grid (without one, the workflow predicts the calibration runs)
assumptions: The plate is thin and reaches a steady state (the 2-D steady heat equation)
The material and the losses are the same in each run
The temperature rise is proportional to the heater power
outputs: The conductivity k, the face and edge losses, the heater efficiency and the spread length, with R-hat and ESS
The error on the calibration run that the fit did not see
The decision: is the calibration good enough?
The predicted temperature of each point for the new layouts, as a map
A report
about.example: Three 10 W test runs give k = 59 W/m/K and a spread length of 13 cm. The run that the fit did not see has an error of 0.12 degC. Thus the workflow predicts the new layout: the hottest point is 33 degC.
about.expert_notes: sci.heat_plate solves A(theta) u = eta q on a finite-volume grid. split.holdout leaves one random run out (leave_group_out, n = 1). model.fit fits the other runs, scores the run held out and fits all the runs again (evaluate_then_refit). The branch needs the holdout RMSE at or below max_error and max R-hat at or below max_rhat. Then model.score predicts the expected field of the layout (posterior draws of the field, without sensor noise).

about.title: Image model check
about.summary_plain: Fits a model that predicts an image and compares its predicted images with the observed image. It shows the differences as maps and writes a report.
use_when: Your model predicts a full image, for example a sky map, a lensed galaxy or a pattern
You want to see where on the image the model does not agree with the data
avoid_when: The observed values are only at a few points (the residual maps are then almost empty)
The model does not predict an image
data_needs: An observed image with two image dims, for example y and x
The model reference, its settings and, if the names are different, the binding of the dataset to the model
assumptions: The model gives predictive draws of the image on the grid of the observed image
The noise of the data is in the predictive draws or in a variable named sigma
outputs: A fitted model version
A table of the parameters with R-hat and the effective sample size
Maps of the observed image, the mean prediction and the residuals
The observed image next to predicted images on one colour scale
The coverage of the 50% and 90% ranges and a report
about.example: A sky map: the normalised residuals look like noise with sd 1.02, 91% of the pixels are in the 90% ranges, and you cannot find the real map in the grid.

references.title: Gabry et al. (2019), Visualization in Bayesian workflow

about.expert_notes: Both plots read the in-sample predictions of the model (source: predictions) with the observed target as observed_data. sci.image_residuals shows the observed image, the mean, the residual and (obs - mean) / sqrt(sd^2 + sigma^2). The recipe adds no sigma to posterior_predictive draws. var selects the image variable when the model has more than one, and frame selects the dim of the slider (for example run or t). The predictive check pools all the pixels. It needs 10 or more predictive draws, and it does not stop the workflow when it fails.

about.title: Network ties: which model?
about.summary_plain: Fits three models of the ties in a network, from shared traits only to a hidden map of the group. Then it compares how well each model predicts, keeps the best one and simulates new networks to compare them with your network.
use_when: You have a table of yes or no ties between the pairs of a group, for example who works with whom
You want to know if shared traits explain the ties, or if the activity of each node and a hidden map are necessary
You need simulated networks to do a check of the model fit
avoid_when: The ties have a direction or are counts
The network has many thousands of nodes (each model looks at every pair)
You need a fast answer (the workflow fits the model three times)
data_needs: A square table with 1 for a tie, 0 for no tie and an empty cell when you do not know
Values for each pair, for example 1 when the two nodes are in the same office
Optional: a group code for each node, for colors in the plots (python -m mapi_plugin_science.export e21 makes this dataset from the law firm data)
assumptions: All three models use the same pairs in the same order
Each pair has a tie or not, and the two directions are the same
Leave-one-pair-out scores (PSIS-LOO) are reliable for these data. The comparison table shows a warning when they are not
outputs: A table that compares the three models (elpd_loo) and their stacking weights
The best model, with the range of each pair effect
A plot of the network with the tie probabilities of the best model
Statistics of simulated networks (density, transitivity and more) with a plot
A report with the plots
about.example: On the coworker network of 71 lawyers, the hidden map predicts best (elpd_loo -761.6, against -763.4 with activity and -894.2 with covariates only). The simulated networks show if the model makes as many triangles as the real network.

references.title: Hoff, Raftery & Handcock (2002), Latent space approaches to social network analysis

about.expert_notes: Bernoulli-logit dyad models: covariates (alpha + x beta), sociality (+ s_i + s_j) and latent_space (- ||z_i - z_j||, Procrustes-aligned). The log-likelihood is over the observed pairs i < j, so the pointwise PSIS-LOO values of the rungs line up for stacking. model.score in simulate mode draws whole graphs from the best rung and returns graph_stat(statistic) for each draw.

about.title: Trait regression across species, with and without the tree
about.summary_plain: Fits the same regression of a species trait four times: once with species as independent points and three times with a family tree that relates them. Then it keeps the version that predicts best and tells you if the effect that you ask about is clearly different from zero.
use_when: You compare a trait across species (or other groups with a known tree) and close relatives are similar
You want to know if an effect stays clear when you include the tree in the model
avoid_when: You have no tree of the species
Fewer than about 20 species (the four versions then predict about equally well)
data_needs: One row for each species: the trait to explain and one or more predictors, all positive (the model takes logs)
The tree in the same dataset: parent(node), branch_length(node), is_tip(node) and tip_label(node), with tip labels equal to the species labels
assumptions: The predictors have a linear effect on the log of the trait
The residuals of related species are correlated as the selected version says (Brownian motion, Pagel's lambda or Ornstein-Uhlenbeck)
outputs: The leave-one-out score (elpd_loo) of the four versions and their stacking weights
The selected model and its slopes, with R-hat and ESS
The decision: is the range of the effect clear of zero?
A plot of the tree with the trait of each species
A report
about.example: Brain size of 301 primates: Pagel's lambda wins (elpd 130, against 15 without the tree). The slope of group size is 0.03, with the 94% range -0.01 to 0.07. Thus the effect is not clear of zero when the model includes the tree.

references.title: Felsenstein (1985), Phylogenies and the comparative method
Pagel (1999), Inferring the historical patterns of biological evolution

about.expert_notes: Four sci.phylo_regression fits that differ only in the residual kind (iid, brownian, lambda, ou) are ranked by PSIS-LOO on the conditional leave-one-out density of each species. select.best keeps the highest elpd_loo, and compare.stacking gives the stacking weights. model.summary reads the slope that focus names from the winner. The branch tests if its HDI excludes zero.

about.title: Disease map: which spatial model?
about.summary_plain: Fits three models of disease counts on a map, from independent areas to areas that share their risk with their neighbours. Then it compares how well each model predicts, keeps the best one and tells you if the effect of your covariate stays clear.
use_when: You have counts and expected counts for each area of a map, and one covariate
You must know if the neighbours of an area change the answer
You need a map of the risk with evidence that the fit is good
avoid_when: You have the location of each case, not counts for each area
The areas have no neighbours (all of them are islands)
You need a fast answer (the workflow fits the model three times. When the effect is clear, it fits the best model two more times)
data_needs: A count of cases and an expected count for each area
One covariate for each area, for example a percentage
An adjacency matrix of the areas and the outline of each area (python -m mapi_plugin_science.export e18 makes this dataset from the Scottish lip cancer data)
assumptions: All three models use the same areas in the same order
The covariate has the same effect in every area
Leave-one-area-out scores (PSIS-LOO) are reliable for these data. The comparison table shows a warning when they are not
outputs: A table that compares the three models (elpd_loo) and their stacking weights
The best model, with the range of the covariate effect and a decision: clear or not clear
Convergence evidence for the best model
When the effect is clear, the range of the effect with wider and narrower priors
A map of the relative risk and a report with the plot
about.example: On the 56 districts of Scotland, the effect of outdoor work on the log risk falls from 0.67 (independent areas) to 0.40 (BYM2) per 10 points when the areas share their risk. The workflow shows which model predicts best and if the effect stays clear.

references.title: Riebler, Sørbye, Simpson & Rue (2016), An intuitive Bayesian spatial model for disease mapping that accounts for scaling
Yao, Vehtari, Simpson & Gelman (2018), Using stacking to average Bayesian predictive distributions

about.expert_notes: Poisson(E_i exp(b0 + b1 x_i + u_i)) with u iid, ICAR or BYM2 (scaled ICAR plus iid with mixing share rho). Each rung stores the pointwise PSIS-LOO values, so compare.stacking solves the stacking weights over the same areas. The branch reads the HDI of b1 on the rung that select.best keeps. When it excludes zero, that rung is fitted again with the prior sds of b0 and b1 and the HalfNormal scale of sigma multiplied and divided by prior_scale.

about.title: Time-series readiness to ARIMAX
about.summary_plain: Finds whether your series needs a difference and how many past values are important. Then it backtests a forecast with drivers against simple benchmarks and keeps the model only if it wins and passes governance.
use_when: You want an automatic, fully tested forecast of one series with drivers
You want a record and an explanation of each decision about the model
avoid_when: You have many related series that affect each other (use VAR or VECM)
You have less than about two seasons of history
data_needs: One numeric series over time, at least two seasons long
Optional drivers that you know for the future (for example, prices and holidays)
assumptions: Past patterns continue into the forecast horizon
The drivers have a linear effect on the series
outputs: Test verdicts and the decision about the difference
The selected AR and MA orders
Backtest errors for each horizon, compared with the benchmarks
A validated ARIMAX model
A plain-language report
about.example: Weekly orders: the tests say 'difference once' and AIC selects (2,1,1). The backtest is 25% better than seasonal naive, and governance passes.

references.title: Hyndman & Athanasopoulos, Forecasting: Principles and Practice

about.title: Series that move together (VAR or VECM)
about.summary_plain: Tests whether several series stay tied together in the long run. Then it makes one model of all the series that keeps the long-run tie or uses their changes.
use_when: Two to five series have an effect on each other (for example, prices, sales and search interest)
avoid_when: A single series
Less than about 50 periods
data_needs: Two to five numeric series over time at the same frequency. Each series has one value for each period (a long table, or a wide sheet that you ingest with the wide mapping)
assumptions: The relationships stay the same over the period
Effects come from past values
outputs: The cointegration rank
A VECM or VAR model
Granger test results
A report
about.example: Your price and the prices of two competitors share one long-run tie. A VECM with rank 1 shows that the gaps close in less than one month.

with.explain_then: The series has a strong seasonal pattern. The workflow compared each value with the same period one season earlier (a seasonal difference).
with.explain_else: The series has no strong seasonal pattern, so the workflow did not apply a seasonal difference.

with.condition: (not nodes.adf.reject or nodes.kpss.reject) and not (nodes.pp.reject and nodes.za.reject) and nodes.overdiff.acf[1] > -0.5
with.explain_then: The tests found that the series wanders and does not return to a steady level. The workflow applied a difference, so the model uses the change from one period to the next.
with.explain_else: The tests found that the series returns to a steady level, or that a difference would go too far. The workflow used the series as it is.
